title: Asked for a Cheaper Incubator, the Embrace Team Made a Sleeping Bag
dek: A Stanford class project became a nonprofit in 2008 when four students chose to keep working on a $200 infant warmer and took it to India.

story.founder: Jane Chen, Rahul Panicker, Naganand Murty and Linus Liang
story.event: Turning a class brief for a cheap incubator into a wax-filled infant warmer, founding a nonprofit and moving it to India
story.summary: In 2007 a Stanford student team asked to design a low-cost incubator instead built a small sleeping bag warmed by a wax-like phase-change pouch, after fieldwork in Nepal. When the partner charities did not take it up, the students incorporated Embrace as a nonprofit in early 2008 and in 2009 moved operations to India. The warmer launched in Bangalore in April 2011 at about $200, against up to $20,000 for an incubator, and was later sold through the for-profit Embrace Innovations.
paragraphs: In the spring of 2007 four Stanford graduate students, Jane Chen, Rahul Panicker, Naganand Murty and Linus Liang, took a course called Entrepreneurial Design for Extreme Affordability. Their brief, from Design that Matters in Boston and Medicine Mondiale in Nepal, was a low-cost incubator. A conventional one could cost $20,000 and needed steady electricity, which many villages did not have.

By the end of the term the team had reviewed the medical research and sent one member to Nepal for fieldwork. "We didn't just take existing incubators and cost-reduce," Chen later said; they tried to imagine other settings, such as the needs of rural mothers. The result was a small sleeping bag holding a pouch of wax-like material that, once warmed, stays near body temperature for hours. Watching rural families in Nepal, the Stanford Daily later reported, led them to plan a version mothers could use at home.

The charities did not take it further. "They wanted a cheaper version of existing baby incubators; we gave them a sleeping bag," Panicker recalled. The students could have gone to well-paid jobs in Silicon Valley. Instead they incorporated Embrace as a nonprofit in early 2008, the year Chen and Panicker became Echoing Green fellows, and won Stanford's Social Entrepreneurship Challenge. Prizes and foundation grants brought the 2009 budget to $400,000.

In early summer 2009 Embrace moved its operations to India, beginning in Hubli, about 250 miles north of Bangalore, with help from the Deshpande Foundation. Panicker left his job at a fibre-optics company that year. Chen travelled through 11 Indian states interviewing doctors, midwives and health officials; focus groups warned against white, the colour of mourning. The expected price rose from about $25 in 2009 to about $200 by launch.

The launch, in April 2011, came from a packaging and quality-control facility in Bangalore. The power failed, the wash tags were misprinted, and the car carrying the first shipment got a flat tyre, so the team hailed a rickshaw. "Everything that could go wrong did," Chen said. Embrace later licensed the warmer to a for-profit company, Embrace Innovations, backed by venture investors, and Panicker said it went through almost 60 versions.

quote.text: Wast thou not a weeping and helpless child, for whom through many nights I sacrificed my sleep? Thou hadst not then the strength thou hast to-day; thou couldst not ward the flies from off thy body.
quote.locator: Chapter VIII, "Concerning Gratitude", "A Mother's Warning to Her Son"
quote.source_title: The Bustān of Sadi, tr. A. Hart Edwards, Project Gutenberg eBook #60471
quote.connection: Saadi's mother reminds a grown son that he was once too weak to brush a fly away, and that someone gave up her sleep for him. Embrace designed for that stage of life, and for the mother awake beside it, rather than for the hospital machine it was asked to copy.

reflection: The brief said incubator, and the students could have delivered one, cheaper and on time. The better answer came from asking who would actually be holding the baby, and where, and then being willing to leave the brief behind.

Most of the people you serve will never see your designs or your plans; they will meet the result on an ordinary, tiring day. It is worth knowing that day as well as you can. And if someone once sat up through nights for you, today may be a good day to tell them you remember.
invitation: Before you next build or fix something for someone, ask them to walk you through the last time they needed it, start to finish, and listen without suggesting anything.

cross_checks.claim: The warmer began as a 2007 Stanford class project, with fieldwork in Nepal, after a brief to design a low-cost incubator
The team chose to continue, founding Embrace as a nonprofit in 2008 with Echoing Green and Stanford prize support
Embrace moved its work to India and launched the warmer from Bangalore in April 2011
The warmer cost about $200 at launch against up to $20,000 for an incubator

research_notes: Move to India: SSIR (Fall 2009) says Embrace moved operations to India in early summer 2009, to Hubli in Karnataka; Open (September 2009) says Panicker quit his job earlier in 2009 and the team was building distribution in India; Stanford GSB (May 2011) says Chen and the team moved to India in 2010; Pomona (2011) and Business Today (2013) place the company in Bangalore by 2011. The story follows the contemporary SSIR account (2009, Hubli first) and says only that the 2011 launch came from Bangalore. The slate's 'moved to Bengaluru in 2008' is not supported: 2008 was the year of nonprofit incorporation. Founding: SSIR gives incorporation in early 2008; LBS (2017) says the warmer launched in 2008, which conflicts with every contemporary source (April 2011 launch), so LBS is cited only for price and background. Price: about $25 expected (SSIR 2009), under $100 (Open 2009), $25 to $100 (GSB 2011), $100 to $200 expected (Stanford Daily 2010), $200 at launch (Pomona 2011; LBS gives around $200); the story says the expected price rose from about $25 to about $200. Incubator cost: up to $20,000 (most sources); Open gives $2,000 to $20,000 and the Stanford Daily $1,000 to $2,000 in developing countries; the story says 'could cost $20,000'. Founders: the slate lists Chen, Panicker and Murty; every source also names Linus Liang, so he is included; Open also mentions Razmig Hovaghimian on the team. Which team member went to Nepal is not named in the sources used, so the story says 'one member'. Murty and Liang later left (Business Today 2013). The Saadi passage is a mother's reproach to an ungrateful son, applied here by analogy to designing for infants and the people who care for them.
